title: Choosing between words, graphs and equations
learning_outcomes: Identify whether a kinematics prompt is best answered with words, a graph or an equation.
Translate the same motion between verbal, graphical and algebraic representations.
Choose the shortest valid method and check that its assumptions fit.
prior_knowledge_summary: Students know controlled definitions of displacement, velocity and acceleration.
Students can use graph gradients and signed areas.
Students can select constant-acceleration equations and complete ideal projectile calculations.
new_learning: Use command words and given data to identify the representation an examiner is testing.
Translate between words, motion graphs and equations without changing the physical model.
Prefer the shortest valid representation and justify why it applies.
not_yet_taught: New force, energy, deformation, waves or electricity relationships.
Motion with air resistance unless a graph supplies the behaviour.
knowledge_boundary: This is a transfer lesson. It reorganises previously taught Kinematics and introduces no later-topic physics.

blocks.title: Three correct routes, one sensible start
body: A lift starts upward, slows, stops and comes down. One student writes a paragraph, one sketches a velocity-time graph and one reaches for an equation. Who has chosen well? Predict before reading on.

The motion is the same, but the task decides the best language. A request to describe needs words, a request to sketch needs a graph, and a request for a value usually needs an equation or graph measurement.

figure.brief: Teacher-sketch visual for contrast three representations, using simple axes, arrows and short labels.
figure.alt_text: A teaching sketch showing contrast three representations.

blocks.title: Read the demand before the data
body: Circle the command word and box the target. State or explain usually needs a physical sentence. Sketch or determine from a graph needs gradients, shapes or areas. Calculate needs a relationship that contains the known quantities and target.

Formal definitions still matter. Displacement is distance in a specified direction from a point. Velocity is rate of change of displacement. Acceleration is rate of change of velocity. These exact ideas tell you what a graph gradient or signed area means.
definitions: distance in a specified direction from a point

figure.brief: Teacher-sketch visual for decision tree from command word, using simple axes, arrows and short labels.
figure.alt_text: A teaching sketch showing decision tree from command word.

blocks.title: One upward trip, translated three ways
body: A package moves upward at 3.0 m s^-1 and slows uniformly to rest in 1.5 s. In words, its upward velocity decreases at a constant rate. On a velocity-time graph, draw a straight line from 3.0 to 0. In equations, a = Δv/Δt = (0 - 3.0)/1.5 = -2.0 m s^-2.

Formula to remember: a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}. Here a is acceleration in m s^-2, Δv is change in velocity in m s^-1 and Δt is the time interval in s. The negative sign means downward acceleration for an upward-positive convention.

figure.brief: Teacher-sketch visual for linked words graph equation triptych, using simple axes, arrows and short labels.
figure.alt_text: A teaching sketch showing linked words graph equation triptych.

blocks.title: Let missing quantities choose the equation
body: For constant acceleration, list u, v, a, s and t. Cross out the quantity neither given nor required. Choose the equation that omits it. This is quicker and safer than trying every formula.

Formula to remember: v = u + at. Formula to remember: s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2. Formula to remember: v^2 = u^2 + 2as. Velocities are in m s^-1, acceleration in m s^-2, displacement in m and time in s. Use one positive direction throughout.

figure.brief: Teacher-sketch visual for known-target equation selector, using simple axes, arrows and short labels.
figure.alt_text: A teaching sketch showing known-target equation selector.

blocks.title: A graph is not just a picture
body: It feels natural to use the height of a velocity-time graph as distance because taller looks like farther. That fails because height is velocity. Displacement comes from signed area under the graph.
Formula to remember: s = \text{area under a velocity--time graph}. Area above the time axis is positive and area below is negative. For total distance, add the magnitudes instead.

figure.brief: Teacher-sketch visual for height versus area misconception, using simple axes, arrows and short labels.
figure.alt_text: A teaching sketch showing height versus area misconception.

blocks.title: Words are shortest for a state
body: Prompt: describe the motion where a horizontal displacement-time graph has zero gradient.
The demand is descriptive and no value is required. Words are shortest: the displacement is constant, so the object is stationary.
Drawing another graph or choosing an equation would add work without adding evidence.

figure.brief: Hand-drawn teacher-sketch summary with a positive axis, compact values, arrows, and only the labels needed for the reasoning.
figure.alt_text: Teacher sketch for words are shortest for a state.

blocks.title: A graph is shortest for a changing pattern
body: Prompt: show velocity during uniform acceleration from 2 m s^-1 to 8 m s^-1 in 3 s.
The demand is to show change over time. A velocity-time graph is shortest: plot (0, 2) and (3, 8), then join them with a straight line.
Words can describe it, but the graph displays initial value, final value and constant gradient together.

figure.purpose: Make the reasoning in a graph is shortest for a changing pattern visible.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn teacher-sketch summary with a positive axis, compact values, arrows, and only the labels needed for the reasoning.
figure.alt_text: Teacher sketch for a graph is shortest for a changing pattern.

blocks.title: An equation is shortest for an exact value
body: Prompt: find displacement when u = 2.0 m s^-1, a = 2.0 m s^-2 and t = 3.0 s.
The demand is numerical and the motion has constant acceleration. Use s = ut + 1/2 at^2.
s = (2.0)(3.0) + 1/2(2.0)(3.0)^2 = 15 m. A scale graph would be slower and less exact.

blocks.title: Use the shortest valid representation
body: First identify the target. Then name the model: definition, graph property, constant acceleration or independent projectile components. Choose words, graph or equation. Finally check signs, units and whether the answer describes the stated interval.

Return to the lift. A description uses velocity direction and change. A sketch shows slopes and axis crossings. A numerical prompt uses graph gradient, graph area or the equation that omits the unwanted quantity. The physics stays fixed while the representation changes.

concepts_taught: Question demand determines whether words, a graph or an equation is the shortest valid representation.
The same motion can be translated consistently between verbal, graphical and algebraic forms.
Model assumptions and known quantities must be checked before selecting a relationship.
misconceptions_addressed: Any constant-acceleration equation may be used without checking known quantities.
A negative answer is automatically wrong.
skills_students_can_now_use: Choose words, graphs or equations efficiently.
words are shortest for a state
a graph is shortest for a changing pattern
an equation is shortest for an exact value
